claims.claim: The gss1 gene was highly expressed in the midgut epithelium of P. xylostella fourth-instar larvae.
claims.source: The gss1 gene was highly expressed in the midgut epithelium, but had very low expression in hemolymph, integument and fat bodies (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The gss1 gene had very low expression in hemolymph, integument and fat bodies of P. xylostella fourth-instar larvae.
claims.source: The gss1 gene was highly expressed in the midgut epithelium, but had very low expression in hemolymph, integument and fat bodies (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: After feeding on A. thaliana Col-0 plants, gss1 expression in larval midgut tissues was approximately 17-fold higher than after feeding on myb28myb29 plants.
claims.source: After feeding on A. thaliana wild-type Col-0 plants containing natural levels of glucosinolates, gss1 expression in larval midgut tissues was approximately 17-fold higher than after feeding on myb28myb29 plants, which lack aliphatic glucosinolates (Figure 1A), suggesting that the expression of this gene is regulated by dietary glucosinolate ingestion.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The expression of gss1 is regulated by dietary glucosinolate ingestion.
claims.source: After feeding on A. thaliana wild-type Col-0 plants containing natural levels of glucosinolates, gss1 expression in larval midgut tissues was approximately 17-fold higher than after feeding on myb28myb29 plants, which lack aliphatic glucosinolates (Figure 1A), suggesting that the expression of this gene is regulated by dietary glucosinolate ingestion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the differential expression data.

claims.claim: gss2 and gss3 showed similar expression patterns to gss1 in P. xylostella larvae.
claims.source: Similar patterns were shown by gss2 and gss3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: Glucosinolates did not induce the expression of several other potential detoxification genes analyzed in the midgut of P. xylostella fourth-instar larvae.
claims.source: However, glucosinolates did not induce the expression of any of several other potential detoxification genes analyzed in the midgut of P. xylostella fourth-instar larvae (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Both columnar cells and basal midgut cells are gss1-positive in P. xylostella.
claims.source: Both the columnar cells and the basal midgut cells are gss1-positive, with white arrows pointing to nuclei of different morphologies.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from FISH experiments shown in Figure 1B-D.

claims.claim: When P. xylostella larvae ingested Col-0 plants infiltrated with the gss1 RNAi construct, gss1 expression in the midgut epithelium was lowered to about 2% of that found in larvae fed on Col-0 plants infiltrated with the empty vector construct.
claims.source: When P. xylostella larvae ingested Col-0 plants (with wild-type glucosinolate levels) infiltrated with the gss1 RNAi construct (Figure 1E), gss1 expression in the midgut epithelium was lowered to about 2% of that found in larvae fed on Col-0 plants infiltrated with the empty vector construct (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: After feeding on myb28myb29 plants, larval gss1 transcript levels were lower than after feeding on Col-0.
claims.source: After feeding on myb28myb29 plants (without aliphatic glucosinolates), larval gss1 transcript levels were lower than after feeding on Col-0, but gss1 silencing on myb28myb29 plants also led to a substantial (63%) transcriptional reduction (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: gss1 silencing on myb28myb29 plants led to a substantial (63%) transcriptional reduction.
claims.source: After feeding on myb28myb29 plants (without aliphatic glucosinolates), larval gss1 transcript levels were lower than after feeding on Col-0, but gss1 silencing on myb28myb29 plants also led to a substantial (63%) transcriptional reduction (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Formation of desulfo-4MSOB from 4MSOB by midgut extracts of gss1-silenced larvae was reduced to less than 50% of that formed by extracts of non-silenced larvae.
claims.source: Formation of desulfo-4-methylsulfinylbutyl glucosinolate (desulfo-4MSOB) from 4MSOB by midgut extracts of gss1-silenced larvae was reduced to less than 50% of that formed by extracts of non-silenced larvae, indicating gss1 expression and GSS activity were both greatly suppressed by the RNAi treatment (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro enzyme assays shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: gss1 expression and GSS activity were both greatly suppressed by the RNAi treatment.
claims.source: Formation of desulfo-4-methylsulfinylbutyl glucosinolate (desulfo-4MSOB) from 4MSOB by midgut extracts of gss1-silenced larvae was reduced to less than 50% of that formed by extracts of non-silenced larvae, indicating gss1 expression and GSS activity were both greatly suppressed by the RNAi treatment (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the enzyme assay data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: gss2 and gss3 were co-silenced by the gss1 RNAi treatment.
claims.source: While gss2 and gss3, like gss1, were co-silenced by the treatment, transcript levels of genes encoding other sulfatases and the sulfatase modifying factor 1 (sumf1) were not influenced by gss1 silencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Transcript levels of genes encoding other sulfatases and sumf1 were not influenced by gss1 silencing.
claims.source: While gss2 and gss3, like gss1, were co-silenced by the treatment, transcript levels of genes encoding other sulfatases and the sulfatase modifying factor 1 (sumf1) were not influenced by gss1 silencing (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from qRT-PCR experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: When fed continuously on Col-0 plants with aliphatic glucosinolates, gss-silenced larvae grew 33% less than non-silenced larvae at six dph.
claims.source: When fed continuously on Col-0 plants with aliphatic glucosinolates, gss-silenced larvae grew 33% less than non-silenced larvae at six dph (days post hatching), and the growth gap continued to widen until eight dph, when gss-silenced larvae were only 64% as heavy as non-silenced larvae before pupation (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from larval weight measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: At eight dph, gss-silenced larvae were only 64% as heavy as non-silenced larvae before pupation.
claims.source: When fed continuously on Col-0 plants with aliphatic glucosinolates, gss-silenced larvae grew 33% less than non-silenced larvae at six dph (days post hatching), and the growth gap continued to widen until eight dph, when gss-silenced larvae were only 64% as heavy as non-silenced larvae before pupation (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from larval weight measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The pupal mortality of gss-silenced insects was nearly 4-fold higher than non-silenced ones.
claims.source: Although pupal weights were not significantly different between treatments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the pupal mortality of gss-silenced insects was nearly 4-fold higher than non-silenced ones (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from pupal mortality measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Female moths from gss-silenced Col-0 larvae laid 56% less eggs than female moths on all other treatments.
claims.source: Female moths from gss-silenced Col-0 larvae laid 56% less eggs than female moths on all other treatments (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from egg-laying measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Male moths arising from gss-silenced larvae fed on Col-0 decreased egg hatching by 36%.
claims.source: Meanwhile, male moths arising from gss-silenced larvae fed on Col-0 did not affect the egg laying capacity of females arising from non-silenced larvae (Figure 2D), but did decrease egg hatching by 36% (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from egg hatching measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: Larvae fed on myb28myb29 plants grew faster and had significantly higher mass than larvae fed on Col-0 plants.
claims.source: Comparing P. xylostella performance on the two plant lines, larvae fed on myb28myb29 plants (without aliphatic glucosinolates) grew faster and had significantly higher mass than larvae fed on Col-0 plants (with aliphatic glucosinolates) (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from larval weight measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Considering only larvae fed on myb28myb29 plants, gss silencing did not cause physiological changes.
claims.source: However, considering only larvae fed on myb28myb29 plants, gss silencing did not cause physiological changes (Figure 2B–H).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from performance measurements shown in Figure 2B–H.

claims.claim: Silencing of gss impacted P. xylostella larval growth and development only in the presence of aliphatic glucosinolates.
claims.source: Therefore, silencing of gss impacted P. xylostella larval growth and development only in the presence of aliphatic glucosinolates, causing pupal mortality and sex-specific effects on adults.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the performance data.

claims.claim: Non-silenced fourth-instar larvae with normal levels of GSS activity desulfated 4MSOB and formed the non-toxic desulfo-4MSOB in the larval midgut epithelium.
claims.source: Non-silenced fourth-instar larvae with normal levels of GSS activity desulfated 4MSOB and formed the non-toxic desulfo-4MSOB in the larval midgut epithelium (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: When GSS activity was lowered by plant-mediated RNAi, levels of desulfo-4MSOB decreased by more than 90%.
claims.source: However, when GSS activity was lowered by plant-mediated RNAi, levels of desulfo-4MSOB decreased by more than 90%, while the concentrations of the toxic hydrolysis product 4MSOB-isothiocyanate (4MSOB-ITC) increased over 10-fold in the midgut of gss-silenced larvae, with a concomitant rise in the hemolymph (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: When GSS activity was lowered by plant-mediated RNAi, the concentrations of 4MSOB-ITC increased over 10-fold in the midgut of gss-silenced larvae.
claims.source: However, when GSS activity was lowered by plant-mediated RNAi, levels of desulfo-4MSOB decreased by more than 90%, while the concentrations of the toxic hydrolysis product 4MSOB-isothiocyanate (4MSOB-ITC) increased over 10-fold in the midgut of gss-silenced larvae, with a concomitant rise in the hemolymph (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Intact 4MSOB became a very prominent peak in gss-silenced larvae.
claims.source: Intact 4MSOB, present only in trace amounts in non-silenced midguts, became a very prominent peak in gss-silenced larvae (Figure 3A), suggesting that plant myrosinases in the P. xylostella midgut lumen are not very efficient, and so may be easily outcompeted by insect GSS in non-silenced insects.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Plant myrosinases in the P. xylostella midgut lumen are not very efficient.
claims.source: Intact 4MSOB, present only in trace amounts in non-silenced midguts, became a very prominent peak in gss-silenced larvae (Figure 3A), suggesting that plant myrosinases in the P. xylostella midgut lumen are not very efficient, and so may be easily outcompeted by insect GSS in non-silenced insects.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Plant myrosinases may be easily outcompeted by insect GSS in non-silenced insects.
claims.source: Intact 4MSOB, present only in trace amounts in non-silenced midguts, became a very prominent peak in gss-silenced larvae (Figure 3A), suggesting that plant myrosinases in the P. xylostella midgut lumen are not very efficient, and so may be easily outcompeted by insect GSS in non-silenced insects.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the metabolite data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: At the end of larval development, P. xylostella retained considerable amounts of 4MSOB-ITC in pupae and adults, 210 and 390 nmol/g, respectively.
claims.source: At the end of larval development, P. xylostella retained considerable amounts of 4MSOB-ITC in pupae and adults, 210 and 390 nmol/g, respectively (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The desulfo-4MSOB remaining was excreted at the prepupal stage.
claims.source: However, the desulfo-4MSOB remaining was excreted at the prepupal stage (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Neither desulfo-4MSOB nor 4MSOB-ITC were detectable in P. xylostella eggs.
claims.source: Neither desulfo-4MSOB nor 4MSOB-ITC were detectable in P. xylostella eggs (Figure 3B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claims.claim: The metabolites of I3M appear to be less toxic than those of 4MSOB to P. xylostella.
claims.source: Nevertheless, the lack of indolic glucosinolate desulfation had no observable negative effects on the performance of P. xylostella larvae (Figure 2). There were no differences between silenced and non-silenced larvae feeding on myb28myb29 plants, which lack aliphatic glucosinolates and contain slightly elevated indolic glucosinolate levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B). Thus the metabolites of I3M appear to be less toxic than those of 4MSOB to P. xylostella, as also observed for other herbivores (Jeschke et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the performance data and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Feeding on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants strongly reduced larval growth.
claims.source: Feeding on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants strongly reduced larval growth (Figure 4A), and pupae of larvae fed on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants suffered 4-fold higher mortality than those feeding on solvent-infiltrated plants (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from complementation experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Pupae of larvae fed on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants suffered 4-fold higher mortality than those feeding on solvent-infiltrated plants.
claims.source: Feeding on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants strongly reduced larval growth (Figure 4A), and pupae of larvae fed on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants suffered 4-fold higher mortality than those feeding on solvent-infiltrated plants (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from complementation experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Female moths of larvae feeding on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants laid approximately 45% less eggs than those feeding on solvent-infiltrated plants.
claims.source: Furthermore, the female moths of larvae feeding on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants laid approximately 45% less eggs than those feeding on solvent-infiltrated plants (Figure 4C), and eggs fertilized by male moths of larvae feeding on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants had approximately 50% lower hatching success (Figure 4F,H).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from complementation experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Eggs fertilized by male moths of larvae feeding on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants had approximately 50% lower hatching success.
claims.source: Furthermore, the female moths of larvae feeding on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants laid approximately 45% less eggs than those feeding on solvent-infiltrated plants (Figure 4C), and eggs fertilized by male moths of larvae feeding on 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated plants had approximately 50% lower hatching success (Figure 4F,H).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from complementation experiments shown in Figure 4F and 4H.

claims.claim: The negative physiological effects suffered by gss-silenced P. xylostella larvae fed on A. thaliana Col-0 plants with aliphatic glucosinolates are likely caused by the exposure to 4MSOB-ITC.
claims.source: Therefore, the negative physiological effects suffered by gss-silenced P. xylostella larvae fed on A. thaliana Col-0 plants with aliphatic glucosinolates are likely caused by the exposure to 4MSOB-ITC resulting from hydrolysis of glucosinolates that were not efficiently desulfated as in non-silenced insects.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the complementation experiments.

claims.claim: When larvae of C. carnea preyed on gss-silenced P. xylostella larvae fed on plants containing aliphatic glucosinolates, significantly greater amounts of 4MSOB-ITC were present in the gut, hemolymph and Malpighian tubules compared to C. carnea preying on non-silenced P. xylostella larvae.
claims.source: When larvae of this lacewing preyed on gss-silenced P. xylostella larvae fed on plants containing aliphatic glucosinolates, significantly greater amounts of 4MSOB-ITC (and significantly lesser amounts of desulfo-4MSOB) deriving from P. xylostella larvae were present in the gut, hemolymph and Malpighian tubules compared to C. carnea preying on non-silenced P. xylostella larvae (Figure 5B,C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claims.claim: The lacewing metabolized a large portion of the 4MSOB-ITC ingested from gss-silenced P. xylostella larvae via the general mercapturic acid pathway.
claims.source: The lacewing metabolized a large portion of the 4MSOB-ITC ingested from gss-silenced P. xylostella larvae via the general mercapturic acid pathway (Figure 5A), an isothiocyanate detoxification pathway used by many organisms (Gloss et al., 2014; Schramm et al., 2012), resulting in 44 nmol/mL and 67 nmol/g of the N-acetylcysteine conjugate of 4MSOB-ITC (4MSOB-ITC-NAC) in the hemolymph and Malpighian tubules, respectively (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5A and 5D, supported by citations.

claims.claim: For C. carnea preying on gss-silenced P. xylostella, 327 nmol/mL 4MSOB-ITC and 116 nmol/mL of 4MSOB-ITC-NAC were detected in the anal secretion.
claims.source: For C. carnea preying on gss-silenced P. xylostella, 327 nmol/mL 4MSOB-ITC and 116 nmol/mL of the detoxification product, 4MSOB-ITC-NAC, were detected in the anal secretion (Figure 5C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claims.claim: The low amount of 4MSOB-ITC remaining in C. carnea larvae was excreted in the pupal pellet during pupation, resulting in undetectable 4MSOB-ITC residues in adults.
claims.source: The low amount of 4MSOB-ITC remaining in C. carnea larvae was excreted in the pupal pellet during pupation, resulting in undetectable 4MSOB-ITC residues in adults (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Lacewing larvae preying on non-silenced P. xylostella larvae feeding on Col-0 plants excreted approximately 320 nmol/g of desulfo-4MSOB in the pupal pellet.
claims.source: Lacewing larvae preying on non-silenced P. xylostella larvae feeding on Col-0 plants with aliphatic glucosinolates excreted approximately 320 nmol/g of desulfo-4MSOB in the pupal pellet, resulting in virtually no detectable desulfo-glucosinolate being retained in adults and the meconium (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from metabolite measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Lacewing larval growth was reduced when feeding on gss-silenced isothiocyanate-containing P. xylostella larvae fed on Col-0 plants compared to non-silenced P. xylostella larvae or P. xylostella larvae fed on myb28myb29 plants.
claims.source: The metabolism of toxic glucosinolate hydrolysis products by C. carnea incurs costs that are visible as a slight delay in its larval development. Lacewing larval growth was reduced when feeding on gss-silenced isothiocyanate-containing P. xylostella larvae fed on Col-0 plants (with wild-type glucosinolates) compared to non-silenced P. xylostella larvae or P. xylostella larvae fed on myb28myb29 plants (without aliphatic glucosinolates) (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from lacewing performance measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Pupation was delayed by about two days for C. carnea larvae fed on the gss-silenced P. xylostella larvae raised on Col-0 plants.
claims.source: Additionally, pupation was delayed by about two days for C. carnea larvae fed on the gss-silenced P. xylostella larvae raised on Col-0 plants, but without affecting the final proportion of larvae successfully reaching the pupal stage (Figure 6B and Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from lacewing performance measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The exposure to isothiocyanates from gss-silenced prey did not affect C. carnea pupal mortality and adult egg-laying capacity.
claims.source: Similarly, the exposure to isothiocyanates from gss-silenced prey also did not affect C. carnea pupal mortality and adult egg-laying capacity (Figure 6C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from lacewing performance measurements shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claims.claim: C. carnea displayed no particular feeding preference towards either gss-silenced or non-silenced larvae fed on either Col-0 or myb28myb29 plants.
claims.source: The ability of C. carnea to detoxify isothiocyanates is also reflected in the fact that its behavior is not much influenced by the glucosinolate processing capacity of its prey. This lacewing displayed no particular feeding preference towards either gss-silenced or non-silenced larvae fed on either Col-0 or myb28myb29 plants (Figure 6E,F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from predation bioassays shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claims.claim: Expression of detoxification-related genes and resulting enzyme activities are induced in the herbivore midgut in response to plant defense compounds.
claims.source: In several cases, expression of detoxification-related genes and resulting enzyme activities are induced in the herbivore midgut in response to plant defense compounds (Adesanya et al., 2017; Kumar et al., 2014; Schweizer et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The GSS detoxification system of P. xylostella is inducible.
claims.source: The GSS detoxification system of the specialized herbivore P. xylostella is therefore also inducible, similarly to the GSS activity previously identified in the generalist-feeding desert locust (Schistocerca gregaria) (Falk and Gershenzon, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The inducibility of GSS can be seen as a way for the herbivore to minimize the physiological costs of detoxification.
claims.source: The inducibility of GSS can be seen as a way for the herbivore to minimize the physiological costs of detoxification.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the biological significance of the findings.

claims.claim: Induced GSS detoxification imposes costs, as inferred from slower larval development when feeding on glucosinolate-containing wild-type plants relative to aliphatic glucosinolate-depleted mutant plants.
claims.source: However, induced GSS detoxification still imposes costs, as inferred from slower larval development when feeding on glucosinolate-containing wild-type plants relative to aliphatic glucosinolate-depleted mutant plants (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: A trade-off between growth and detoxification capacity has been noted for other insect herbivores feeding on glucosinolate-containing plants.
claims.source: A trade-off between growth and detoxification capacity has also been noted for other insect herbivores feeding on glucosinolate-containing plants.
claims.evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Several generalist lepidopteran caterpillars resist glucosinolate poisoning by metabolizing isothiocyanates to their corresponding glutathione conjugates.
claims.source: Several generalist lepidopteran caterpillars resist glucosinolate poisoning by metabolizing isothiocyanates, the chief toxic products of glucosinolate hydrolysis, to their corresponding glutathione (GSH) conjugates.
claims.evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: The cost of biosynthesizing the GSH necessary for isothiocyanate detoxification leads to delayed larval development in generalist lepidopteran caterpillars.
claims.source: However, the cost of biosynthesizing the GSH necessary for isothiocyanate detoxification leads to delayed larval development (Jeschke et al., 2016b; Jeschke et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: RNAi is less efficient in lepidopterans than in other insect orders.
claims.source: Nevertheless, it has been documented that RNAi is less efficient in lepidopterans than in other insect orders and gives rise to varying effects in different species (Shukla et al., 2016; Terenius et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Exogenous dsRNA is readily degraded in Heliothis virescens larvae.
claims.source: Previous studies on Heliothis virescens revealed that exogenous dsRNA is not only readily degraded, but also lacks intracellular transport in larvae, reducing the efficiency of RNAi (Shukla et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Exogenous dsRNA lacks intracellular transport in Heliothis virescens larvae.
claims.source: Previous studies on Heliothis virescens revealed that exogenous dsRNA is not only readily degraded, but also lacks intracellular transport in larvae, reducing the efficiency of RNAi (Shukla et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: P. xylostella has been successfully silenced by feeding droplets of dsRNA.

claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: P. xylostella has been successfully silenced by bacterially produced dsRNA.

results.result: The gss1 gene is highly expressed in the midgut epithelium of P. xylostella larvae and its expression is induced by dietary glucosinolate ingestion. Expression is approximately 17-fold higher after feeding on glucosinolate-containing Col-0 plants compared to myb28myb29 plants lacking aliphatic glucosinolates, with similar patterns observed for gss2 and gss3.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59 are well-supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 1A) and FISH experiments (Figure 1B-D) showing tissue-specific expression patterns and glucosinolate-dependent induction. The data demonstrate clear differential expression between plant genotypes and tissue types with appropriate statistical analysis.

results.result: Plant-mediated RNAi successfully silenced gss genes in P. xylostella, reducing gss1 expression to ~2% of control levels and GSS enzyme activity to <50% of control. The RNAi construct co-silenced gss1, gss2, and gss3 but did not affect other sulfatases.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C66 and C114-C115 are strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence including qRT-PCR (Figure 1F), in vitro enzyme assays (Figure 1G), and specificity controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 4). The silencing efficiency is well-documented with appropriate controls and statistical validation.

results.result: Silencing of gss genes severely impaired P. xylostella performance only in the presence of aliphatic glucosinolates, causing 50% reduction in larval growth, 4-fold increase in pupal mortality, >50% reduction in egg laying by females, and 36% reduction in egg hatching when males were exposed to ITCs.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C74 and C117-C121 are well-supported by comprehensive performance data (Figure 2) showing glucosinolate-dependent effects with appropriate statistical analysis. The sex-specific reproductive effects are documented, though the bimodal egg hatching pattern warrants further investigation as acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: Silencing of gss resulted in >90% reduction in desulfo-4MSOB and >10-fold increase in toxic 4MSOB-ITC in larval midgut and hemolymph. Substantial intact 4MSOB accumulated in gss-silenced larvae, suggesting inefficient plant myrosinase activity that is normally outcompeted by insect GSS.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C83 and C116 are strongly supported by comprehensive LC-MS/MS metabolite profiling (Figure 3) across multiple tissues and life stages. The data clearly demonstrate the metabolic consequences of gss silencing with appropriate quantification and controls.

results.result: Complementation experiments using 4MSOB-ITC-infiltrated myb28myb29 plants recapitulated the negative effects of gss silencing, demonstrating that 4MSOB-ITC is responsible for reduced larval growth, 4-fold increased pupal mortality, 45% reduced egg laying, and 50% reduced egg hatching.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C89 are well-supported by complementation experiments (Figure 4) that phenocopy the gss silencing effects. The experimental design appropriately tests the causal role of 4MSOB-ITC, though the authors acknowledge limitations of the infiltration approach.

results.result: C. carnea larvae preying on gss-silenced P. xylostella ingested elevated 4MSOB-ITC and metabolized it via the mercapturic acid pathway, producing 4MSOB-ITC-NAC conjugates that were excreted in anal secretion and pupal pellet, resulting in undetectable residues in adults.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are strongly supported by comprehensive metabolite profiling (Figure 5) across multiple C. carnea tissues and excretions. The data clearly demonstrate the detoxification pathway and excretion routes with appropriate quantification.

results.result: Feeding on gss-silenced P. xylostella containing elevated ITCs caused reduced larval growth and ~2-day delayed pupation in C. carnea, but did not affect pupal mortality, adult egg-laying capacity, or prey preference.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 and C46 are well-supported by comprehensive C. carnea performance data (Figure 6) showing transient developmental costs without long-term fitness consequences. The behavioral assays appropriately demonstrate lack of prey avoidance.

results.result: Silencing glucosinolate sulfatase genes resulted in systemic accumulation of toxic isothiocyanates that impaired P. xylostella larval development and adult reproduction, establishing that glucosinolate desulfation is beneficial to the herbivore despite its metabolic cost.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 and C41-C45 represent the main conclusions supported by the integrated evidence from gene silencing, metabolite profiling, and performance assays. The conclusion that desulfation is beneficial is well-justified by the severe fitness consequences of gss silencing.

results.result: C. carnea efficiently detoxified ingested isothiocyanates via the mercapturic acid pathway with no negative effects on survival, reproduction, or prey preference, demonstrating that both herbivore and predator possess independent detoxification mechanisms with benefits to reproductive fitness.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 and C47-C52 represent the main conclusions about predator responses, supported by metabolite profiling, performance assays, and behavioral experiments. The claim of 'no negative effects' is slightly overstated given the observed growth delay, but the lack of long-term fitness effects is well-documented.

results.result: Plant defenses and their detoxification strongly influence herbivore fitness but might only subtly affect the third trophic level.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 represent the overarching conclusion supported by the differential impacts on P. xylostella (severe) versus C. carnea (transient). The use of 'might' appropriately acknowledges the limited scope to a single predator-prey system.

results.result: The GSS detoxification system of P. xylostella is inducible by dietary glucosinolates, which can be seen as minimizing physiological costs, though induced detoxification still imposes costs as evidenced by slower larval development on glucosinolate-containing plants.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are supported by the expression data (Figure 1A) and performance comparisons between Col-0 and myb28myb29 plants (Figure 2A). The interpretation of inducibility as cost-minimization is reasonable though somewhat speculative.

results.result: Desulfation in P. xylostella is a genuine detoxification reaction that increases performance and reproductive fitness, consistent with evolutionary evidence of positive selection. Similar desulfation reactions in other herbivores likely also function as genuine detoxification measures.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C127 are supported by the experimental data and evolutionary context from cited work. The extrapolation to other species (C124-C127) is appropriately qualified as 'likely' and supported by citations.

results.result: P. xylostella larvae possess additional adaptations beyond desulfation to avoid glucosinolate toxicity, including inefficient myrosinase activity in the gut. GSS may inhibit myrosinase through substrate diversion and sulfate-mediated inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 are supported by the detection of intact glucosinolates in gss-silenced larvae (Figure 3A), but C130 regarding myrosinase inhibition by sulfate is speculative and only supported by a citation. The mechanism of myrosinase inefficiency requires further investigation.

results.result: The metabolites of indolic glucosinolate I3M appear to be less toxic than those of aliphatic glucosinolate 4MSOB to P. xylostella.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 is supported by the lack of performance effects on myb28myb29 plants containing elevated indolic glucosinolates (Figure 2) and the instability of I3M-ITC (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), consistent with cited literature.

results.result: gss-silenced P. xylostella larvae retained approximately 450 nmol/g 4MSOB-ITC in midgut and ~300 nmol/mL in hemolymph, representing at least a 10-fold increase over non-silenced larvae. C. carnea ingested lower ITC levels than herbivores feeding directly on glucosinolate-containing plants.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C141 are supported by metabolite quantification (Figure 3) and comparison with literature values for sequestering insects. The comparison appropriately contextualizes the predator exposure levels.

results.result: Insect herbivores frequently metabolize plant defense compounds, but the physiological and ecological consequences are not fully understood, and it has rarely been studied whether such metabolism is genuinely beneficial.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 accurately represent the state of knowledge and research gap that motivated the study. These are appropriately supported by the literature context.
